Affront

/ə-FRONT/ — stress on second syllable, rhymes with font · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To affront someone is to insult them or offend their dignity, usually through disrespectful words or behavior.

Serving the guest of honor last was taken as a deliberate affront.

Worked Example

A diplomat was seated below junior staff members at an official state dinner — a calculated slight intended to diminish her nation's standing.

Affront captures both the deliberate nature and the targeting of someone's dignity or honor. It is more precise than 'insult' (which could be accidental) or 'embarrassment' (which lacks the intentionality aimed at status).

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

snub: A snub is disrespect by omission — coldly ignoring someone, refusing a greeting, leaving them off the list. An affront is the opposite kind of act: open and active, a deliberate word or deed flung at someone's dignity. A snub freezes a person out; an affront strikes at them.

disrespect: Disrespect is the broad term for treating someone as unworthy of courtesy — an attitude that can show up in many small ways over time. An affront is a single, deliberate act: one calculated blow aimed at a person's dignity or honor. Disrespect is the climate; an affront is the lightning strike.

indignity: An indignity is humiliating treatment as the person on the receiving end experiences it — being searched, kept waiting, talked over. An affront is the same injury seen from the offender's side: a deliberate act aimed at someone's dignity. Indignity names the suffering; affront names the attack.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

honor: to show public respect for someone

compliment: to praise someone sincerely and kindly

Where it sits · how pointed the attack on dignity — rudeness → insult → slight → affront

rudeness vs. affront: Rudeness is far weaker than an affront: rudeness is general bad manners aimed at no one in particular, while an affront is a deliberate act aimed straight at a person's dignity.

insult vs. affront: An insult is weaker than an affront; an insult is hurtful words that can wound anyone's feelings, but an affront is an open, often public act that strikes at someone's honor and standing.

slight vs. affront: A slight is weaker than an affront: a slight wounds dignity in a small, deniable way — a forgotten introduction, a seat at the far end of the table — while an affront is an open, unmistakable blow to someone's honor.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — af-

Prefix — af-: to, toward (form of ad-) (Latin)

Root — front (frons, frontem)

Root — front (frons, frontem): forehead, face (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: An affront is literally an insult delivered 'to the face' — Old French afronter even meant 'to slap in the face.' The word keeps that idea of open disrespect: an affront offends someone's dignity right in front of them, out in the open.

Use the root in a new word: confront

Use the root in a new word: confront: She turned to confront her accuser face to face — the same Latin root front, 'forehead, face,' that makes an affront an insult thrown at someone's face.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / literary

Affront is a formal word for calculated, intentional insult aimed at someone's honor or standing. Use it when the disrespect is clearly deliberate and touches on status or dignity. For everyday rudeness, 'insult' is simpler and sufficient.
